Use this page when your cohort is built and you want to analyse the time until
the outcome: Kaplan-Meier curves, a Cox model for the hazard ratio, the check of
proportional hazards, and what to do when death (or another event) can come
first. Time-to-event analysis (survival analysis) handles the fact that not
everyone reaches the event during follow-up (censoring). You need the
analysis-ready dataset with follow-up time and event status from [Phase
12](joins.qmd#follow-up-time); when you are done you have curves and estimates
to take through [output control](export.qmd).

*Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own.*
`survival`, `survminer` and `tidycmprsk` must be installed in your R environment
on DST (Statistics Denmark).

## Starting point

You need two things per person: **follow-up time** (how long the person was
followed) and **event status** (whether the event/outcome occurred in that time:
1 = yes, 0 = censored, i.e. not seen during follow-up). Follow-up time is **stop
date minus index date**, where the stop date is the first of outcome, death,
emigration or end of study; see [Calculate follow-up time and event
variable](joins.qmd#follow-up-time) in Phase 12 for the construction
itself.

```r
library(survival) # Surv(), survfit(), coxph(), cox.zph()

df <- readRDS("path/to/analysis.rds") # analysis-ready dataset, one row per person (per person and index date if matched with replacement)

# Surv() combines time + status into one "survival object" used by all the models:
#   time_days = days from index to event OR censoring (whichever comes first)
#   outcome   = 1 if the event occurred, 0 if the person was censored
# We build the object here ONLY to see what Surv() produces:
survival_obj <- Surv(time = df$time_days, event = df$outcome)
survival_obj # view the object: a "+" marks a censored person (e.g. 12+)

# In practice you don't need to store it: in the models below you write
# Surv(...) directly in the formula. It is shown here only for understanding.
```

## Kaplan-Meier curves

`survfit()` computes the Kaplan-Meier estimate (the event-free proportion over
time), and `ggsurvplot()` draws it nicely.

```r
library(survminer) # ggsurvplot()

fit <- survfit(
  Surv(time_days, outcome) ~ exposure, # one curve per exposure group
  data = df
)

ggsurvplot(
  fit,
  data = df,
  pval = TRUE, # show the log-rank test p-value
  conf.int = TRUE, # show confidence bands around the curves
  risk.table = TRUE, # table below the figure: number at risk over time
  xlab = "Days since index", # axis labels
  ylab = "Event-free proportion"
)
```

With simulated numbers the curves look like this (here the exposed drop faster,
i.e. they get the outcome more often):

![Kaplan-Meier curves with simulated data. `ggsurvplot()` typically also adds a risk table below the figure.](images/km_example.png)

::: {.callout-warning}
## Before you export a Kaplan-Meier curve

The curve and its risk table are output like any table. Each step in the curve
is one or a few events, and each number at risk is a table cell, so check them
against the small-cell rule (3 or 5, see [Export](export.qmd#figures-and-curves)).
In the tail of the curve, where few people are left, this usually fails: one way
out is to cut the x-axis (`xlim =` in `ggsurvplot()`) where the number at risk
falls below your threshold.

One minus the Kaplan-Meier curve also overestimates the risk when a competing
event (typically death) can preclude your outcome: see [Competing
risks](#competing-risks) below.
:::

## Cox regression (hazard ratio)

`coxph()` gives hazard ratios (HR) adjusted for covariates.
`tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE)` shows them as HRs instead of log-hazards.

```r
library(gtsummary) # tbl_regression()

# Without replacement (each person appears only once): an ordinary Cox model.
cox <- coxph(Surv(time_days, outcome) ~ exposure + age + sex, data = df)

cox %>% # pass the model on to a clean table
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) # exponentiate = TRUE -> hazard ratios
```

A hazard ratio is a ratio of rates (hazards) over follow-up: 1 = no difference,
above 1 = higher rate in the exposed, below 1 = lower. It is not a ratio of
risks. See [Reading your
result](regression.qmd#read-the-output).

**The difference with replacement.** If the comparison cohort is matched **with
replacement** (or there is crossover), the same person appears several times and
the rows are not independent. Then you add one argument, `cluster = pnr`, to
exactly the same model. It does not change the hazard ratio estimate; it
replaces the standard errors with robust (sandwich) standard errors that allow
for the repeated person, so the confidence intervals are no longer too narrow. Same idea
as in [Regression](regression.qmd#clustered-standard-errors).

```r
# With replacement (same person several times): the ONLY difference from the model above is cluster = pnr.
coxph(
  Surv(time_days, outcome) ~ exposure + age + sex,
  data = df,
  cluster = pnr
) %>% # <- the only change: cluster on person id
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) # HR unchanged; only the CIs become correct (usually wider)
```

Note the syntax: `coxph()` takes the cluster variable as an **argument** without
a tilde (`cluster = pnr`), whereas `sandwich::vcovCL()` on the
[Regression](regression.qmd#clustered-standard-errors) page uses a
**formula** with a tilde (`cluster = ~ pnr`). Same idea (cluster on person id),
just two functions' different ways of receiving the variable.

**Stratified on the matched set.** To compare each exposed person only with
their own matched comparison persons, add `strata(match_id)` (the matched-set id
from [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd)): each matched set then gets its
own baseline hazard.

```r
coxph(Surv(time_days, outcome) ~ exposure + strata(match_id), data = df, cluster = pnr) %>% # cluster = pnr only if people repeat across sets
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) # factors matched on exactly are constant within a set, so the strata already handle them
```

::: {.callout-note}
**What is your time scale?** The time axis (what the x-axis shows on e.g. a
Kaplan-Meier curve) is a choice. By default it is **time since index** - how
long each person has been followed since their own start date (that is
`time_days` in the examples). But you can also follow people on:

- **attained age**: so the model compares people at the **same age**. That
  adjusts for age automatically and flexibly (a strong confounder for most
  outcomes), without you having to model the shape of age yourself. Common in
  register studies.
- **calendar time**: if the calendar period itself matters (e.g. treatment that
  has changed over the years).

Time since index is simplest; age-as-time-scale is often stronger when risk is
driven heavily by age. Technically you choose the time scale via what you put in
as time in `Surv()`. With age as time scale, each person enters at their age at
index (**delayed entry**), so `Surv()` needs both entry and exit age -
`Surv(age_at_exit, outcome)` alone would count everyone as at risk from birth:

```r
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    age_at_exit = age + time_days / 365.25 # age = age at index, in years with decimals (from Phase 12)
  )
coxph(Surv(age, age_at_exit, outcome) ~ exposure + sex, data = df) # age is the time axis, so not a covariate
```
:::

## Check the assumption: proportional hazards

The Cox model assumes **proportional hazards** (PH): that the hazard ratio is
constant over follow-up. If it is not, a single hazard ratio does not describe
an effect that changes over time. Check it with `cox.zph()`, which is based on
the scaled Schoenfeld residuals (in short, whether the effect drifts over time).

```r
ph <- cox.zph(cox) # formal PH test per variable + global
print(ph) # small p-value = evidence against proportional hazards
plot(ph) # residual curve per variable; a sloping curve
#   indicates a non-proportional hazard
```

With register-sized data the test has the power to flag even a tiny departure,
so a small p-value alone says little. Judge the plot: how much the curve slopes,
and whether that changes what you would conclude.

<details>
<summary>What to do if the assumption is violated</summary>

If a variable violates the assumption, you can e.g. **stratify** on it (`+ strata(variable)` in the model, giving it its own baseline hazard) or **model a time-dependent effect** (let the effect change over follow-up).

A third alternative is to **drop the hazard ratio** and use **RMST** (*restricted mean survival time*): the average event-free time within a fixed window (e.g. "months alive within 5 years"). You compare groups by the **difference in RMST**, measured in **time units** instead of a ratio, and it is valid even when PH is violated. In R: the `survRM2` package.

</details>

## Competing risks {#competing-risks}

::: {.callout-warning}
If another event can preclude your outcome (classically death, before the
outcome can occur), it is a *competing risk*. One minus the Kaplan-Meier curve
then overestimates the risk, because it treats those who died as if they were
merely censored and could still get the outcome later. In register cohorts with
older people or long follow-up this is common.
:::

Each person ends up in one of three places, and only the first thing that
happens counts: (1) they never reach an event during follow-up (*censored*), (2)
they get your outcome, or (3) they have the competing event (e.g. death).
Someone who dies first can never reach the outcome, and the analysis must
reflect that.

### 1. Set up the data

You need the same two variables as for an ordinary Cox model - but the status
variable now takes **three values** instead of two (so we call it `status`
instead of `outcome`):

- `time_days` - the time from index to the **first** thing that happens
  (outcome, death or end of follow-up).
- `status` - **what** happened: censored, outcome or death.

`status` must be a **factor**, and `tidycmprsk` requires **"censored" to be the
first level**. The order of the levels is also where you tell R which level is
your outcome and which is the competing risk:

```r
library(tidycmprsk) # cuminc(), crr()

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    status = factor(
      status_code, # your raw code, one value per person (e.g. 0/1/2)
      levels = c(0, 1, 2), # the order sets the meaning:
      labels = c(
        "censored", #   1st level = censored (MUST be first)
        "outcome", #   2nd level = your outcome (the one crr models)
        "death"
      ) #   3rd level = the competing risk
    )
  )
```

You build `status_code` (0/1/2) from the dates - what happened *first*: 0 =
censored (e.g. end of follow-up, emigrated or otherwise lost), 1 = outcome, 2 =
death. The construction lives in [Calculate follow-up time and event
variable](joins.qmd#follow-up-time) (Phase 12). The *number* you give
censoring does not matter - what matters is that the censored level is listed
**first** in `levels =` (which is why it is 0 here).

### 2. Describe the risk over time (CIF)

**Instead of Kaplan-Meier**, use the **cumulative incidence function** (CIF,
also called Aalen-Johansen). It allocates people correctly across the competing
outcomes, so death no longer "steals" risk from the outcome. (This is about the
*curve*; the regression itself is still done with Cox, see step 3.)

```r
# Surv(time, status) with the factor status -> cumulative incidence for EACH event type:
cuminc(
  Surv(time_days, status) ~ exposure, # one curve per exposure group
  data = df
) # also gives Gray's test for a group difference
```

### 3. Regression: pick the model to match your question

There are two regression models, and they answer different questions:

- **The rate of the outcome among those still alive and event-free:** run an
  ordinary Cox model and censor the competing event. You do that by setting the
  event to `status == "outcome"`: both censored and dead people then become "no
  event". This is the *cause-specific* hazard, which is better suited to an
  etiological question ([Lau, Cole & Gange
  2009](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwp107)).
- **The cumulative incidence (absolute risk) of the outcome:** use
  **Fine-Gray** (`crr`), where the dead stay in the risk set. `crr` by default
  models the first event type after "censored" (here "outcome") and treats the
  rest ("death") as competing. This is the *subdistribution* hazard.

```r
# Etiology - cause-specific Cox: status == "outcome" turns death (and censored) into "no event"
coxph(
  Surv(time_days, status == "outcome") ~ exposure + age + sex,
  data = df
) %>%
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) # -> cause-specific hazard ratio

# Absolute risk - Fine-Gray: uses the factor status directly (outcome vs. competing)
crr(Surv(time_days, status) ~ exposure + age + sex, data = df) %>%
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) # -> subdistribution hazard ratio
```

Neither hazard ratio is a risk ratio. The subdistribution hazard ratio tells
you the direction in which the exposure shifts the cumulative incidence (if the
model fits), but not by how much; for the absolute risk, report the cumulative incidence (CIF) at
fixed time points, for example at 1 and 5 years.

<details>
<summary>Rule of thumb: which one do I pick?</summary>

If you want to describe or predict risk (e.g. "what is the 5-year risk of the outcome?"), use the CIF and Fine-Gray. If you want to know whether the exposure changes the rate of the outcome in those still at risk, use the cause-specific Cox. Many studies report both.

</details>

## Time-varying covariates (briefly)

If a variable changes during follow-up (e.g. a blood test or body mass index, BMI), it cannot be
a single value per person. It must be in **start/stop format** (one row per
interval), built with `survival::tmerge()` and analysed with
`coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, outcome) ~ ...)`. The reshaping itself is in
[Time-varying variables](time-varying.qmd).
